text.p: Twenty-three people in careers ranging from dance to biology were awarded nearly $6 million in no-strings-attached "genius grants" on Monday by the MacArthur Foundation.

The grants range from $150,000 to $375,000, disbursed over a five-year period. The latest awards brought to $158 million the amount of money handed out by the foundation since the unusual programme began 16 years ago.

The winners are chosen by an anonymous panel which does not accept applications and which seeks out achievers in a wide variety of fields. The winners are free to spend the money any way they please and do not need to report back to the foundation, which also provides them with health insurance.
The latest winners:
Luis Alfaro, 35, Los Angeles, $230,000, a performance artist, playwright and poet who "dramatizes issues concerning identity and social power."
Lee Breuer, 60, New York, $355,000, a writer and playwright whose most recent work combines the story of Peter Pan with Scottish folk music, Bunraku puppetry and Javanese shadow puppetry.
Vija Celmins, 58, New York, $345,000, an artist whose paintings and prints "show a remarkable singularity of vision, independent of trends in the art world."
Eric Charnov, 49, Summit Park, Utah, $300,000, a biologist whose mathematical models support much of current understanding of foraging behaviour and the evolution patterns of gender.
Elouise Cobell, 51, Blackfeet Indian Reservation, Montana, $310,000, a businesswoman who organised the first tribal-owned Native American bank in the United States.
Peter Galison, 42, Cambridge, Massachusetts, $265,000, a researcher into the history of science who focuses on the role of scientific instruments.
Mark Harrington, 37, New York, $240,000, policy director of the Treatment Action Group who has advanced the knowledge of AIDs treatments.
Eva Harris, 31, San Francisco, $210,000, a biologist whose work in technology transfer has facilitated disease treatment in Central and South America.
Michael Kremer, 32, Cambridge, Mass., $215,000, an economist "whose models provide clear and accessible answers in lucid and original ways."

Russell Lande, 45, Eugene, Ore., $280,000, a biologist whose analyses "have shown how standard forestry and wildlife practices, if continued at current rates, will have a devastating impact on biodiversity."
Kerry Marshall, 41, Chicago, $260,000, a painter specialising in depicting the lives of lower-middle-class and middle-class blacks in the United States.
Nancy Moran, 42, Tucson, Arizona, $265,000, an ecologist and evolutionary biologist who has specialised in research on the relationship between aphids and their host plants.
Han Ong, 29, New York, $200,000, a playwright and performer "who evocatively depicts the realities of life in urban, multicultural America."

Kathleen Ross, 56, Toppenish, Washington, $335,000, president and co-founder of Heritage College, which was formed in cooperation with the Yakima Indian Nation and most of whose students are the first native Americans in their families to attend college.

Pamela Samuelson, 48, Berkeley, California, $295,000, a lawyer who is considered a master of intellectual property law who has become a "crucial link in policy discussions among the legal, information technology, and telecommunications communities."
Susan Stewart, 45, Philadelphia, $280,000, a cultural and literary critic whose writing draws from anthropology, folklore, history and cultural studies.
Elizabeth Streb, 47, New York, $290,000, a dancer and choreographer who uses natural or amplified body impact sounds as her only "music."
Trimpin, 45, Seattle, $280,000, a musician and scuptor who creates sound and music-making machines with computers and junked mustical instruments.
Loic Wacquant, 36, Berkeley, California, $235,000, a sociologist who has written extensively on urban poverty, including research into the social world of a boxing gym in Chicago.
Kara Walker, 27, Providence, Rhode Island, $190,000, an artist who uses a silhouette technique to explore racial, physical and sexual exploitation.
David Wallace, 35, Bloomington, Illinois, $230,000, author of "The Broom of the System" and "Infinite Jest" whose fiction stands out for inventive wordplay and intellectual rigour.
Andrew Wiles, 44, Princeton, New Jersey, $275,000, a mathematician who in 1994 found proof of "Fermat's Last Theorem," which had challenged number theorists for 350 years.
Brackette Williams, 46, Tucson, Arizona, $285,000, an anthropologist whose work has included an in-depth study of ritual and symbolism in Guyana.
